title: The Quran Verse That Saved Muhammad | Surah 66 Explained
description:
In the previous episode of the Allah-Who? series we examined a verse from Surah Al-Ahzab that appeared to address a very personal situation in Muhammad’s household. That raised an important question: when revelation appears to solve the Prophet’s personal circumstances, where exactly is it coming from?
In this episode we examine Surah 66 (Surah At-Tahrim) — one of the most debated passages in the Quran.
Modern explanations often present a harmless story about honey, but early historical sources and classical tafsir literature tell a very different story involving Maria al-Qibtiyya, a slave woman who came into Muhammad’s household as a gift from the Egyptian ruler Al-Muqawqis.
According to several classical narrations, an incident involving Maria and Muhammad triggered a domestic conflict with Hafsa, leading to the revelation of Surah 66:1-5.
In this video we examine:
• the historical background of Maria al-Qibtiyya
• the story preserved in early Islamic sources
• the honey explanation presented in modern tafsir
• the linguistic and contextual clues within Surah 66 itself
• and the broader question of how revelation interacts with the personal life of the Prophet.
This video is part of the ongoing Allah-Who? series where we analyze passages of the Quran that raise historical and theological questions.
If you’ve searched for Surah 66 explained, Muhammad and Maria story, Quran Surah Tahrim meaning, or Tafsir Surah 66, this video gives you the rational perspective.
Don’t forget to subscribe, like, comment, and share if you enjoy content that asks difficult questions about religion, history and scripture.

transcript: In the previous episode, we examined a single verse from Surah Al-Ahzab, a verse that on the surface appears simple, almost ordinary. Guests had stayed too long after Muhammad's wedding feast. The prophet felt shy asking them to leave, and then suddenly a revelation appeared telling them not to remain in his house. In the same passage, another instruction appeared. People were told to speak to his wives from behind a curtain, and the verse ended by declaring that after the prophet's death, no one would ever be allowed to marry his wives. Three separate situations, [music] one revelation. When we step back and look at it carefully, the question becomes difficult to ignore. Why does divine revelation repeatedly appear in moments that resolve the prophet's personal circumstances? That question brings us to the next chapter because Surah 66, At-Tahrim, takes us even deeper into the private world of Muhammad's household. This time, the issue is not dinner guests. It is a conflict inside his own marriage. The opening verse immediately sets the scene. Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you seeking to please your wives? In a single line, the Quran presents us with an extraordinary image. The creator of the universe, the being who's supposed to govern galaxies, stars, and the laws of existence >> [music] >> has stepped directly into a domestic dispute inside one man's home. Now, here is a strange part. If you read modern explanations of this chapter, you will almost never hear the story that early historians recorded. Instead, you're given a much safer, softer, and a harmless version. A story about honey. But the original story that triggered these verses is far more explosive. According to this version, Muhammad used to drink honey at the house of one of his wives. Two other wives became jealous of the extra time he spent there. So, when he visited them, they told him that his breath smelled unpleasant after drinking it. Wanting to keep peace in the household, Muhammad reportedly promised that he would stop consuming honey. And then, revelation arrived. Allah intervened to defend the honey. But, if we pause for a moment, an obvious question appears. The Quran is supposed to be a book of moral guidance for all humanity until the end of time. So, what moral lesson would humanity learn from this episode? That honey is allowed? If that explanation were true, eternal creator of billions of galaxies would be revealing scripture simply to confirm that someone may continue drinking honey. Do we really need divine revelation from the creator of the universe for something as simple as that? Something about that explanation does not fit the scale of the claim. And when we turn to the early historical reports and classical tafsir literature, the story becomes far less innocent. The honey story begins to look suspiciously like damage control because many early sources connect these verses not to honey, but to a woman named Maria al-Qibtiyya. Maria did not simply appear in Muhammad's household by chance. Her story begins with a letter. Around the late 620s, Muhammad sent letters to several rulers outside Arabia inviting them to accept Islam. The other option that he gave them was that if they didn't accept, they would be attacked. One of those letters was sent to the ruler of Egypt known in Islamic sources as Muqawqis. Muqawqis did not convert to Islam, but he responded politely for he had heard of Muhammad and knew him well. And so, along with his reply, he sent gifts. Among those gifts were two Coptic slave woman. One of them was Maria al-Qibtiyya. [music] Maria was then brought to Medina and entered Muhammad's household as a slave girl. According to many sources, Muhammad developed a relationship with her, and that relationship eventually triggered events behind sura 66. According to the historical reports, Muhammad had a system to manage time with his wives. Each wife had a designated day with him. In other words, a rotation schedule. One day for one wife, the next day for another. Now, one day, when it was Hafsa's turn with the prophet, Muhammad apparently sent Hafsa to her father, Umar, saying that he wanted to see her. So, Hafsa left for her paternal home. While she was gone, Muhammad had a private encounter with Maria inside Hafsa's room, on her own bed. When Hafsa found out that she hadn't been called for, she returned home immediately. And what did she see when she entered the house? The prophet and his slave girl on her own bed. Both of them were caught red-handed during the act. An argument followed. Hafsa was furious. Any woman would be right if she found her husband in bed with another woman. So, she made a big hue and cry over the issue. In order to calm the situation, Muhammad reportedly promised her that he would not see Maria again. He also asked her to keep the matter secret. He specifically told Hafsa not to tell Aisha because Aisha would get angry if she heard about this incident. But, a secret did not remain secret for long. Hafsa confided in Aisha, and then all hell broke loose. Then, Aisha informed the other wives, and they all revolted against him. Muhammad was so cornered that he did not approach his wives for 29 days, a month in the Islamic calendar. But, he could not stay away for long. >> [music] >> And suddenly, the private politics of the prophet's household became the subject of revelation. Allah understood Muhammad's predicament and immediately sent down a verse. Before we continue with the story, there is one important detail that helps us understand the situation. In early Islamic law, sexual relations [music] with female slaves owned by a man were considered permissible. This was not unique to Muhammad. It is part of the broader social system of the time. But in the Quran, there is also verse that specifically addresses the prophet's [music] own circumstances. In Surah 33:50, Muhammad's given explicit permission regarding certain categories of women. Among them are those whom your right hand possesses, a phrase used in Quran to refer to female slaves. [music] In other words, the text itself states that women who come into prophet's possession as slaves [music] were lawful to him to have a sexual relationship with. This is important context for the story we are examining. Maria al-Qibtiyya was not one of Muhammad's wives. She was a slave woman who had come into his household after being sent as a gift. And under the rules described in Quran itself, a woman in that position was considered permissible for the prophet. Which means the conflict that erupted as house was not about whether Muhammad was legally allowed to be with Maria. The conflict was about something much [music] more human. Jealousy. Now, the opening words of Surah 66 begins to make sense. Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking to please your wives? This verse appears to address the promise Muhammad had just made. The verse continues, Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths. >> [music] >> In other words, the promise Muhammad made in the heat of that argument could now be set aside. A divine instruction had arrived explaining that he was no longer bound by it. And this raises an even deeper moral question. Not only does the revelation release the prophet from a promise he made to his wife, it also implicitly supports the continuation of her relationship with a slave woman. If the Quran is meant to guide humanity morally for all time, why would the creator of the universe intervene in [music] a way that reinforces the institution of slavery rather than questioning it? The chapter then describes how the secret spread between the wives. The prophet confided something to one of them and she disclosed it to another. According to the verse, Allah informed Muhammad that the information had been passed along. Apparently, the God was also keeping track of the gossip network inside Muhammad's household. Then the tone shifts. Two of the wives are warned. The verse says that if they unite against him, Allah himself will support the prophet. And then comes a line that completely changes the atmosphere of the chapter. He divorces you, perhaps his Lord will replace you with wives better than you. Imagine hearing that during a marital dispute. Another curious detail appears when we examine the historical reports surrounding this episode. Hafsa's father was Umar Khattab. Some narration say that during his conflict, Umar himself warned his daughter not to compete with Aisha for the prophet's attention. He reportedly told her that if Muhammad divorced her, Allah would give him wives better than her. Later, we find a verse in the Quran making almost exactly the same >> [music] >> statement. Perhaps that is coincidence, but it's not the first time we have seen something like this. Just in the previous episode, we saw that Umar had suggested stricter separation around the prophet's wives and later a verse appeared instructing believers to speak to [music] them from behind a curtain. First, a suggestion, then an incident, then revelation. And there is another important piece of the story. After the revelation in Sura 66 told Muhammad not to forbid what was lawful to him, the promise he had made to Hafsa was effectively canceled [music] and the relationship with Maria continued. In fact, the only son Muhammad ever had, Ibrahim, was born from that relationship. So, the sequence becomes very clear. A domestic conflict erupts. A promise is made to calm an angry wife. His wife informs the rest of his household. A fight erupts. Muhammad stays away from his wives for a month. The promise becomes inconvenient. Revelation arrives explaining that the promise does not need to be kept. The wives are warned, and the relationship that caused the conflict continues. When we place all these pieces together, the honey explanation begins to look less like history and more like a later attempt to soften an uncomfortable story. If this was simply about honey, why would the Quran respond with warnings to the wives, references to broken promises, and even threats of divorce and replacement? Honey is simple. Concubines are complicated. Especially when the narrative suggests that divine revelation intervened to release the prophet from a promise he had just made. Now, step back and look at the larger pattern. >> [music] >> In Surah Al-Ahzab, revelation appeared to resolve an awkward social situation at a wedding feast. Here, in Surah Al-Tahrim, revelation appears in the middle of a household dispute. And in both cases, the outcome aligns remarkably well with the prophet's immediate interests. At some point, we have to ask uncomfortable question. When revelation repeatedly appears exactly where the prophet needs it, the real question is not what God said. The real question is, who is actually speaking? Because if a religious leader today claimed that God conveniently revealed instructions supporting his personal relationships, his domestic authority, and his broken promises, most people would immediately recognize what was happening. Yet, when the same pattern appears in ancient scriptures, many are told not to ask questions, but questions are exactly what honest reading requires. Because when the words of God repeatedly solve the problems of one man, the line between divine revelation and human convenience begin to blur. And once you notice that pattern, it becomes very difficult to unsee it. >> [music] >> Which brings us back to the question that started this entire series. When the Quran speaks in these moments, who is really speaking? Allah or Muhammad? So, who was the real Allah? Allah who? If you found this explanation thought-provoking, consider subscribing to the channel and sharing this video with someone who enjoys asking difficult questions. Because this investigation is far from over. There are many more passages in the Quran which raises awkward questions. And in the upcoming episodes of Allah who, we will continue examining them one by one. Until then, it's bye for now from Pale Blue Thoughts.
